name: Heroin and fentanyl (street opioids)
oneLiner: Leaving methadone treatment was linked to about three times the death rate of staying on it: 36.1 versus 11.3 deaths per 1,000 person-years.

axes.classification: DSM-5: opioid use disorder. ICD-11: 6C43 disorders due to use of opioids (code not verified against the WHO browser this pass).

safety.text: Coming back after a break is where death risk concentrates: after prison, rehab or a detox, tolerance is gone, and the first two weeks back carry 3 to 8 times the drug-death risk of the weeks after. Fentanyl makes every dose a gamble. Keep naloxone where others can reach it, and do not use alone.

timeline.label: Acute withdrawal: aches, cramps, sweats, runny nose, diarrhoea, vomiting, gooseflesh
timeline.note: Short-acting opioids (heroin): starts within about 12 h of a missed dose, peaks at 36-72 h (48 h drawn as a midpoint), eases over the next 4-7 days. Overall 5-14 days depending on half-life. Methadone: milder but can last 2 weeks or more; buprenorphine: milder, similar length.

timeline.label: Anxiety, restlessness, irritability, insomnia
timeline.note: Listed among acute withdrawal symptoms; the source gives no separate time course for mood and sleep, so the acute window is reused. Months-long low mood and poor sleep: see placeholders.

markers.label: Buprenorphine taken within 24 h of fentanyl: 5.2 times the odds of severe (precipitated) withdrawal
24-48 h after fentanyl the odds are still 3.4 times higher; methadone showed no such effect
Worst of the physical withdrawal: 36-72 h
Fentanyl took a mean 7.3 days to clear urine (one person 19 days) in 12 people in residential treatment
After a break (prison, rehab), weeks 1-2 back carry 3-8 times the drug-death risk of weeks 3-12. Counted from release, not from last use.

beliefs.voice: Methadone is just swapping one drug for another.
beliefs.science: It replaces a street drug with a dosed medicine, and that keeps people alive: across 19 cohorts, deaths were 11.3 per 1,000 person-years on methadone and 36.1 off it.
beliefs.beliefSource: 06-opioids-stimulants.md sections 4-5: verbatim 'I know it's drug replacement but it's the only thing that gives me a sense of normalcy' (r/OpiatesRecovery); findings from PMC13060028 ('replacing one drug for another') and PMC9394166 ('legal heroin').

beliefs.voice: I'll do a detox, get clean, and that's it.
beliefs.science: A detox removes tolerance but rarely ends use. In one London follow-up, all three overdose deaths after inpatient detox were in the group that completed it. Mortality rises in the weeks after leaving treatment.
beliefs.beliefSource: 06-opioids-stimulants.md section 5.1: family pressure to come off methadone, then relapse (verbatim, r/OpiatesRecovery); PMC11157918: 'It just felt like I'd wasted that time coming off the methadone.'

beliefs.voice: I've been clean for months. I know my dose.
beliefs.science: The old dose no longer matches your tolerance. Across six prison systems, drug-related death risk in the first two weeks after release was 3 to 8 times that of weeks 3 to 12.
beliefs.beliefSource: 06-opioids-stimulants.md section 3: 'Because obviously I was clean and I didnae realise how clean I was, know what I mean, the high risk.' (PMC11157918, verbatim-attested).

beliefs.voice: Suboxone will throw me straight into hell withdrawal.
beliefs.science: It can, if taken too soon after fentanyl: severe withdrawal odds rose about fivefold within 24 hours. But in hospital starts only 11.5% had precipitated withdrawal (16.3% with confirmed fentanyl), and methadone did not cause it.
beliefs.beliefSource: 06-opioids-stimulants.md section 3 (findings only, PMC10039575): people refuse to carry naloxone for fear of being revived into withdrawal. A study of the same fear about buprenorphine starts: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Staying on methadone or buprenorphine long term
whatWorks.note: Retention cuts all-cause and overdose deaths. The riskiest stretches are the first 4 weeks on methadone and the weeks after leaving either drug. WHO: agonist maintenance has the strongest evidence of effectiveness.

whatWorks.what: Naloxone carried by the people around you
whatWorks.note: Reverses an opioid overdose if given in time; WHO recommends it for anyone likely to witness one. Being revived can mean instant withdrawal, which puts some people off carrying it.

whatWorks.what: A plan for the first weeks after any break
whatWorks.note: Prison, rehab and detox all drop tolerance. People leaving jail said starting medication only 2-3 days before release was too late; using alone right after release was named as the fatal combination.

whatWorks.what: Timing buprenorphine starts around fentanyl with a clinician
whatWorks.note: Severe precipitated withdrawal is more likely within 48 h of fentanyl use; methadone does not carry this effect.

numbers.stat: About 125,000 people died of opioid overdose worldwide in 2019 (WHO estimate).
Overdose deaths: 2.6 per 1,000 person-years on methadone versus 12.7 off it (pooled cohorts, searched to 2016).
Drug-related death risk is 3 to 8 times higher in weeks 1-2 after prison release than in weeks 3-12 (6 studies, 69,093 person-years).

name: Prescription opioid painkillers
oneLiner: Among people on opioids for chronic pain, addiction averaged 8-12%; physical dependence is expected with long-term use and is not the same thing.

axes.classification: DSM-5: opioid use disorder; tolerance and withdrawal do not count toward it when the opioid is taken solely under appropriate medical supervision. ICD-11: 6C43 (code not verified this pass).

safety.text: Do not stop a long-term prescription suddenly or cut it fast. After tapers, emergency visits for overdose or withdrawal were 1.57 times and mental-health crises 1.52 times as frequent as before. CDC advises cuts of 10% a month or slower after a year or more of use. Keep naloxone at home.

timeline.label: Acute withdrawal: aches, cramps, sweats, gut upset, gooseflesh
timeline.note: Short-acting opioids such as oxycodone and hydrocodone: within about 12 h, peak 36-72 h (48 h drawn), easing over 4-7 days. Methadone can run 2 weeks or more; buprenorphine is milder with similar length. On a slow taper, smaller bouts follow each cut.

timeline.label: Anxiety, irritability, insomnia
timeline.note: Part of the acute symptom list; no separate time course in the source.

markers.label: Worst of the physical withdrawal: 36-72 h
8 weeks after a buprenorphine taper ended, success fell to 8.6% (49.2% while on it)

beliefs.voice: My doctor prescribed it, so it can't be addiction.
beliefs.science: Partly right. Dependence and withdrawal are expected with long-term use and do not count as addiction under DSM-5. But across 38 chronic-pain studies, addiction averaged 8-12% and misuse 21-29%.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced: no verified first-person quote or cognition study for this belief was found in this pass.

beliefs.voice: If I come off, the pain will be unbearable.
beliefs.science: Evidence is very low quality but points one way: in fair-quality studies, pain, function and quality of life improved after dose reduction. CDC notes improvements after slow, voluntary reductions; fast cuts carry their own risks.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

beliefs.voice: A two-week taper and I'm done.
beliefs.science: In a 653-patient trial, a 2-week buprenorphine taper worked for 6.6%. During 12 weeks of treatment 49.2% did well; 8 weeks after tapering off, 8.6% still did.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Buprenorphine maintenance once opioid use disorder has developed
whatWorks.note: In the POATS trial of prescription-opioid patients, success was 49.2% during extended treatment versus 6.6% after a short taper.

whatWorks.what: Slow, agreed tapers: 10% a month or slower after a year or more
whatWorks.note: CDC 2022. Slow or pause the taper if withdrawal appears. Abrupt stops are unlikely to be worth the risk unless there are warning signs of overdose.

whatWorks.what: Naloxone kept at home
whatWorks.note: WHO recommends naloxone for anyone likely to witness an overdose.

whatWorks.what: Interdisciplinary pain programmes and buprenorphine-assisted reduction
whatWorks.note: Several intervention types may help people reduce; overall evidence quality very low.

numbers.stat: Addiction 8-12% and misuse 21-29% among chronic-pain patients prescribed opioids (38 studies).
After tapering from 50+ MME a day, overdose-or-withdrawal visits rose 1.57-fold and mental-health crises 1.52-fold, 12-24 months on (21,515 tapers, US claims 2008-2017).
POATS trial: 49.2% success on buprenorphine at week 12; 8.6% eight weeks after tapering off.

name: Kratom
oneLiner: Kratom is a plant whose main alkaloid acts on opioid receptors; in a survey of 293 regular users in Malaysia, more than half had severe dependence.

axes.classification: No named diagnosis. Assessed with DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria; 'kratom use disorder' is a proposed label. No specific ICD-11 code found.

safety.text: Leaf kratom withdrawal is usually mild to moderate. The bigger risks are mixing and concentrated 7-OH products: fentanyl was a cause in most kratom-positive overdose deaths, and 7-OH is a potent opioid the DEA moved to schedule in July 2026.

beliefs.voice: Kratom is natural, so it's safe.
beliefs.science: Natural says nothing about dependence. Its main alkaloid is a partial opioid agonist. In 2016-2017, 91 US overdose deaths listed kratom as a cause, nearly all alongside other drugs.
beliefs.beliefSource: Aly and Grundmann 2026 review (r3): in an ecological momentary assessment study, users rated kratom as safer than other substances.

beliefs.voice: I'm using kratom to get off opioids, so it's treatment.
beliefs.science: Many use it that way: in a US survey of 8,049 users, 68% took it for pain and many for opioid withdrawal. But evidence that it treats opioid addiction comes only from small observational studies.
beliefs.beliefSource: Grundmann 2017 survey (r5), recruited partly through American Kratom Association channels, so likely skewed favourable.

beliefs.voice: Kratom withdrawal is nothing.
beliefs.science: For leaf kratom, studies describe mild to moderate, short withdrawal. But frequent use drives dependence: more than half of regular Malaysian users scored severe. Concentrated extracts carry higher risk.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Opioid-use-disorder medicines (mostly buprenorphine) for moderate to severe kratom use disorder
whatWorks.note: 14 case reports plus a survey of addiction specialists, 89.5% of whom had used buprenorphine. No trials.

whatWorks.what: Steer clear of concentrated 7-OH products and tell your doctor what you take
whatWorks.note: Clinicians are advised that 7-OH products carry significantly greater risks than traditional kratom.

numbers.stat: 152 of 27,338 US overdose deaths (0.56%) tested positive for kratom, July 2016-Dec 2017; kratom was a cause in 91, and the only substance detected in 7.
Any fentanyl was listed as a cause of death in 65.1% of those kratom-positive deaths.

name: Alcohol
oneLiner: Alcohol withdrawal can begin 6-24 hours after the last drink, with seizures most likely around 24 hours: stopping a heavy daily habit is a medical event.

axes.classification: DSM-5: alcohol use disorder. ICD-11: 6C40 disorders due to use of alcohol (code not verified this pass).

safety.text: If you drink heavily every day, stopping suddenly can kill: withdrawal seizures (8-48 h) and delirium (from day 2 to day 5) are emergencies, and each withdrawal tends to be worse than the last. Get assessed before you stop. Most people can withdraw outside hospital with medication and monitoring; those at high risk of seizures or delirium should be admitted.

timeline.label: Early withdrawal: anxiety, poor sleep, headache, nausea, sweating, fast pulse
timeline.note: Signs begin 6-24 h after stopping or cutting down. ASAM ties emergence, peak and resolution of mild withdrawal to a 6-36 h window; 24 h is a drawing midpoint, not a sourced peak. In moderate or severe cases symptoms continue into the rows below.

timeline.label: Seizure window
timeline.note: Can strike without other obvious withdrawal signs.

timeline.label: Hallucinations
timeline.note: Develop within 12-24 h; typically resolve within 24-48 h if delirium does not follow.

timeline.label: Withdrawal delirium (DTs): acute confusion
timeline.note: ASAM gives 72-96 h after the last drink in one passage and 24-48 h (up to 3-5 days) in another; usually lasts 2-3 days. Drawn from 48 h to cover both.

timeline.label: Lingering irritability, anxiety and poor sleep
timeline.note: ASAM: protracted symptoms 'can persist for weeks'. No upper limit given; 4 weeks is a drawing length, not a sourced end.

timeline.label: Cue-triggered craving grows rather than fades
timeline.note: Male inpatients in China tested at 7, 14, 30 and 60 days: cue craving was highest at 60 days, the last point measured, so the true peak may be later.

markers.label: Mild withdrawal, low risk: severe withdrawal is unlikely to develop after 36 h
Delirium (DTs) window: 72-96 h in one ASAM passage, from 24-48 h up to day 5 in another
Day 4: symptoms lift and 'maybe it wasn't that bad' arrives (one clinician's account, not a study)
Day 60: cue-triggered craving measured at its highest

beliefs.voice: I'll just stop on my own this weekend.
beliefs.science: A weekend is the danger window: seizures cluster at 8-48 hours and delirium can start from day 2 to day 5. Most people can withdraw outside hospital, but with medication and monitoring, not alone.
beliefs.beliefSource: 14-harm-reduction-moderation.md section 7: two self-managed tapers, one 'because I live alone and I didn't want to risk DTs' (HAMS testimonial).

beliefs.voice: I only drink beer and wine, not the hard stuff.
beliefs.science: A 12-ounce beer at 5%, a 5-ounce glass of wine at 12% and a 1.5-ounce shot at 40% each hold about 14 grams of pure alcohol. The body counts ethanol, not the bottle.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced: no study of beverage-type beliefs was fetched this pass.

beliefs.voice: Maybe my drinking wasn't that bad.
beliefs.science: Possibly: 90% of US excessive drinkers did not meet dependence criteria. But dependence is not the bar for harm. WHO says no drinking is risk-free; alcohol caused about 2.6 million deaths in 2019.
beliefs.beliefSource: 11-youtube-longform.md T15 (Dr Donald Crowe, 'Second Act Recovery', day 4): 'Maybe the drinking wasn't that bad. Maybe I overreacted.'

beliefs.voice: If I can't quit forever, there's no point trying.
beliefs.science: Abstinence is not the only route. A meta-analysis of 22 studies (4,204 patients) found controlled drinking a viable goal, especially with targeted therapy. Unsupported moderation did worse than abstinence.
beliefs.beliefSource: 11-youtube-longform.md T15 (day 2): '"How am I supposed to do this forever?" That thought can break people.'

beliefs.voice: Detox will sort me out.
beliefs.science: Detox treats withdrawal, not drinking. ASAM states withdrawal management alone is not an effective treatment for alcohol use disorder. Medicines help next: acamprosate prevents one return to drinking per 12 people treated.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Medically supported withdrawal for anyone physically dependent
whatWorks.note: Usually benzodiazepine-based and monitored. UK guidance: consider assisted withdrawal above 15 units a day or AUDIT 20+, inpatient above 30 units a day or after past seizures or DTs.

whatWorks.what: Acamprosate or naltrexone
whatWorks.note: 122 trials: one return to any drinking prevented per 12 treated with acamprosate, per 20 with oral naltrexone; naltrexone also prevents one return to heavy drinking per 12.

whatWorks.what: AA and twelve-step facilitation
whatWorks.note: Cochrane 2020: high-quality evidence that manualized AA/TSF beats other established treatments such as CBT for abstinence.

whatWorks.what: Supported moderation when abstinence is not the goal
whatWorks.note: No significant difference from abstinence goals in randomised trials (OR 1.32, CI 0.51-3.39), a wide interval: underpowered, not proof of equivalence.

numbers.stat: About 2.6 million deaths were caused by alcohol in 2019; about 400 million people (7% of those aged 15+) live with alcohol use disorders.
Contact with treatment ranges from under 1% to no more than 14% of people with alcohol use disorders, by country.
90% of US excessive drinkers did not meet criteria for alcohol dependence (NSDUH 2009-2011, 138,100 adults).

name: Benzodiazepines (alprazolam, diazepam, clonazepam and others)
oneLiner: Physical dependence on benzodiazepines can develop within weeks, and stopping suddenly can cause seizures and delirium; the safe way off is a slow taper.

axes.classification: DSM-5: sedative, hypnotic, or anxiolytic use disorder. ICD-11: 6C44 (code not verified this pass). Physical dependence is an expected effect of use and is listed separately from use disorder.

safety.text: Never stop a daily benzodiazepine suddenly: rapid cuts can cause life-threatening seizures and delirium, and seizures have come 1-12 days after stopping. Taper with a prescriber, usually starting with 5-10% cuts every 2-4 weeks. Mixing with alcohol or opioids raises overdose risk; deaths involving benzodiazepines rose nearly tenfold since 2000.

timeline.label: Acute withdrawal (abrupt stop): tremor, palpitations, racing heart, sensory hypersensitivity
timeline.note: Describes stopping, which guidelines advise against; on a taper, smaller bouts follow each cut. Onset about 2-3 days after a short-acting drug, about 7 days after a long-acting one (uncited UK GP reference). Acute symptoms expected to fade once the drug clears, roughly 4-6 weeks. Peak not sourced.

timeline.label: Anxiety, irritability, insomnia
timeline.note: Hard to tell apart from the condition the drug was prescribed for coming back. Same timing caveats as the row above.

timeline.label: Seizure window
timeline.note: Grand mal seizures 1-12 days after discontinuing. In one US hospital series of 82 acute withdrawals, 10% had seizures and none died.

timeline.label: Protracted withdrawal in some: anxiety, depression, poor memory, tinnitus, insomnia
timeline.note: Some patients have symptoms for months or years; Ashton estimated 10-15% of long-term users. Long-term, high-dose, short-acting use raises the risk; slow tapers may lower it. One year drawn; can be longer.

markers.label: Seizure window opens: reported 1-12 days after stopping
Around 4-6 weeks the drug should be cleared; symptoms past this count as protracted

beliefs.voice: My doctor prescribed it, so I can stop whenever I want.
beliefs.science: After under a month at low doses, often true. Beyond that, daily use can cause physical dependence within weeks, and guidelines warn against stopping abruptly: rapid cuts can trigger seizures and delirium.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

beliefs.voice: Cold turkey gets it over with faster.
beliefs.science: Faster is riskier, not shorter. Abrupt stops can cause life-threatening seizures and may raise the risk of protracted symptoms. Trials using 25% weekly cuts lost many patients; guidelines cap cuts at 25% per two weeks.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

beliefs.voice: If I come off, I'll be wrecked for years.
beliefs.science: It happens to some: protracted symptoms can last months or years, and Ashton estimated 10-15% of long-term users. Most do not, and a slow taper with CBT improves the chance of getting off.
beliefs.beliefSource: Joint guideline 2025 (r1): cites a 1,200-person online survey (Reid Finlayson et al.) recruited from benzodiazepine-withdrawal support sites; its patient panel stressed recognising protracted withdrawal.

beliefs.voice: A pill and a couple of drinks is fine.
beliefs.science: Benzodiazepines raise the risk of overdose and death, particularly combined with alcohol or opioids. Fatal overdoses involving them rose nearly tenfold since 2000, often alongside opioids.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: A slow, flexible taper agreed with the prescriber
whatWorks.note: Start with 5-10% cuts every 2-4 weeks and adjust to how it goes. Switching to a longer-acting drug first is optional; guidelines disagree. Strong recommendation, but from clinical consensus with low-certainty evidence.

whatWorks.what: CBT alongside the taper
whatWorks.note: Cochrane: CBT plus taper beat taper alone at 4 weeks (RR 1.40) and 3 months (RR 1.51); the edge was not sustained at 6 months and beyond.

whatWorks.what: Inpatient or residential care for high-risk cases
whatWorks.note: Consider it after past withdrawal seizures or delirium, with unstable illness, or heavy alcohol use (cross-tolerance).

whatWorks.what: A tailored letter from the GP
whatWorks.note: One trial of 322 people: a tailored letter beat a generic one at 12 months (RR 1.70).

numbers.stat: 54% of 1,200 people recruited from withdrawal-support websites reported suicidal thoughts or attempts after stopping (self-selected convenience sample).
82 hospital cases of acute withdrawal at one US centre, 2009-2016: 10% seizures, 3 intubations, no deaths.
9.1% of US adults used a benzodiazepine in the past year (NSDUH 2023), and more than 15% of them reported misuse.

name: GHB and GBL
oneLiner: GHB withdrawal can start within hours of the last dose and slide into delirium; Australian hospital guidance says anyone at risk of severe withdrawal should be admitted.

axes.classification: Diagnosable under DSM-5 and ICD-11 substance categories; whether GHB sits under the sedative or the 'other substance' code was not verified this pass.

safety.text: Do not come off daily GHB or GBL at home. Withdrawal can begin within hours, progress to delirium and seizures, and has killed. Hospital guidance admits anyone at risk of severe withdrawal. Overdose risk climbs when it is mixed with alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, stimulants or ketamine.

timeline.label: Withdrawal: tremor, sweating, racing heart
timeline.note: Can begin 30 minutes to a few hours after the last dose. Severe cases can last 2-15 days in intensive care, up to 2-3 weeks overall. Dosing under 4 hours apart, waking at night to dose, or high daily amounts predict severe withdrawal. Severe withdrawal has followed as little as 7-10 days of frequent dosing.

timeline.label: Anxiety, agitation, profound insomnia
timeline.note: Insomnia in 58% and tremor in 67% of 57 published withdrawal episodes.

timeline.label: Delirium and hallucinations
timeline.note: Delirium in 53% of 38 published cases, typical of heavy users; hallucinations in 63% of 57 episodes. Onset hour not established; 6 h is when one clinical slide deck says severe withdrawal becomes possible.

timeline.label: Relapse risk stays high for months
timeline.note: Relapse after detox has run as high as 60% within 3 months.

markers.label: Symptoms can appear within 30 minutes to a few hours of the last dose
More than 6 h since the last dose: severe withdrawal possible
Only minor symptoms 24-48 h after last use: hospital guidance says admission is not needed
Up to 60% relapse within 3 months of detox

beliefs.voice: G is clean: no hangover, and I've got my dosing down.
beliefs.science: UK records list 159 GHB/GBL-linked deaths from 1995 to 2013. GHB alone was implicated in 37%; alcohol, other drugs, or both in the rest. The authors urge caution with alcohol, benzodiazepines, opiates, stimulants and ketamine.
beliefs.beliefSource: Peterson, Morrison and Lundin 2026 qualitative synthesis (r8): theme 'perceiving GHB as manageable and benign' across 11 studies.

beliefs.voice: I'll come off at home. It's a few rough days.
beliefs.science: GHB withdrawal can turn to delirium fast: 53% of published heavy-user cases did. Seizures and muscle breakdown each occurred in 7% of 57 episodes. Guidance: admit anyone at risk of severe withdrawal.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

beliefs.voice: Once I'm through detox, I'm done.
beliefs.science: Relapse after GHB detox has run as high as 60% within 3 months. In one open-label trial, baclofen after detox cut relapse to 24% from 50% with usual care.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Medically managed detox, in hospital for anyone at risk of severe withdrawal
whatWorks.note: Hospital toxicology guidance; no randomised trials exist. Large, frequent doses of sedating medicines are usually required.

whatWorks.what: Tapering with pharmaceutical GHB rather than benzodiazepines
whatWorks.note: Matched comparison of 84 patients across two countries: less withdrawal and less delirium (2.5% vs 20%) with the GHB taper. Not randomised.

whatWorks.what: Baclofen after detox to prevent relapse
whatWorks.note: Open-label, non-randomised, 107 patients: relapse 24% vs 50%; lapses not reduced. Needs randomised trials.

numbers.stat: 159 GHB/GBL-associated deaths in UK records, 1995 to September 2013; mean age 32; 82% male.
Delirium in 20% of patients tapered with benzodiazepines versus 2.5% tapered with pharmaceutical GHB (84 matched patients, Belgium and Netherlands).
Relapse as high as 60% within 3 months of detox.

name: Gabapentin and pregabalin
oneLiner: On its own gabapentin rarely causes addiction, but among people taking opioids it was linked to 49% higher odds of dying from an opioid overdose.

axes.classification: No named diagnosis; problem use would fall under DSM-5 'other (or unknown) substance use disorder' (not verified this pass). Addiction is rare without a prior substance problem.

safety.text: Do not stop suddenly: withdrawal has started 12 hours to 7 days after stopping, and US drug-safety guidance says to taper. The bigger danger is mixing: with opioids or other sedatives these drugs can cause serious breathing problems, and with opioids the odds of opioid death rose 49%.

timeline.label: Window in which withdrawal has started (case reports)
timeline.note: From 18 case reports, mostly people taking over 3,000 mg a day with past alcohol, cocaine or opioid problems. Symptoms, peak and duration are not summarised in the abstract.

beliefs.voice: It's not addictive. It's for nerve pain.
beliefs.science: Largely true without an addiction history: a 106-study review found few cases. But misuse ran at 15-22% among people who misuse opioids, and pregabalin looked more addictive than gabapentin.
beliefs.beliefSource: Smith, Havens and Walsh 2016 review (r4): gabapentin 'has been presumed to have no abuse potential'.

beliefs.voice: It's safe with my opioids or methadone.
beliefs.science: Among Ontario opioid users, recent gabapentin raised the odds of opioid-related death by 49% (adjusted OR 1.49). FDA warns of serious breathing problems with opioids or other sedatives.
beliefs.beliefSource: Gomes et al. 2017 (r2): 'gabapentin is widely perceived as safe'.

beliefs.voice: I can just stop taking it.
beliefs.science: Withdrawal has been reported 12 hours to 7 days after stopping, and labelling advises tapering before stopping. During alcohol withdrawal, unrecognised gabapentin withdrawal can make standard treatment fail.
beliefs.beliefSource: not sourced.

whatWorks.what: Review any combination with opioids or other sedatives
whatWorks.note: Case-control evidence of higher opioid-death odds, plus FDA warning on breathing problems in people with these risk factors.

whatWorks.what: Taper with the prescriber instead of stopping
whatWorks.note: Labelling advice; no trials of taper schedules found.

whatWorks.what: Avoid, or prescribe under strict monitoring, for people with a substance use history
whatWorks.note: Recommendation from a systematic review, based on who develops addiction.

numbers.stat: Gabapentin misuse: about 1% in the general population, 15-22% among people who misuse opioids.
12.3% of opioid-related deaths versus 6.8% of matched opioid users had recent gabapentin (Ontario 1997-2013; adjusted OR 1.49).
